sources: Saguaro National Park Trails Illustrated map

trails.trailTip: This loop is also open to the one-way Cactus Forest Drive, so stick to the marked footpath and watch for cyclists where the trail parallels the road.
trails.didYouKnow: The Rincon Mountain District's Cactus Forest holds some of the densest stands of saguaro in the entire park.

trails.trailTip: Carry all the water you'll need — Douglas Spring itself is frequently dry, and there is no shade for most of the route; start at first light in warmer months.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail climbs into the Rincon foothills, transitioning from saguaro-studded desert scrub into oak-juniper woodland.

trails.trailTip: This is one of the longest sustained ridge hikes in the park with almost no shade — avoid it entirely on summer afternoons and carry more water than feels necessary.
trails.didYouKnow: The ridge is named for a Tohono O'odham tribal leader and offers views stretching from the Tucson Mountains to the Santa Catalinas.

trails.trailTip: A shaded wash section partway through makes this a good midday option even when it's warm.
trails.didYouKnow: The loop passes the site of a small early-1900s homestead in a wash lined with mesquite and desert hackberry.

trails.trailTip: Please don't touch or trace the petroglyphs — skin oils accelerate erosion of the rock art.
trails.didYouKnow: The petroglyphs at the summit were pecked into volcanic rock by the Hohokam people roughly 800 years ago.

trails.trailTip: The old Gould Mine ruins partway up are fenced off and unstable — view them from the trail rather than climbing on the structures.
trails.didYouKnow: King Canyon follows an old mining and ranching route up toward Wasson Peak, the highest point in the Tucson Mountain District.

trails.trailTip: There is no shade and no water source along the ridge — this is a serious undertaking in anything but cool weather.
trails.didYouKnow: The trail climbs from saguaro-dominated desert up through successive vegetation zones toward the pine-forested Rincon high country.

trails.trailTip: A popular sunset walk in the Tucson Mountain District — arrive with time to spare since the small trailhead lot fills up in the evening.
trails.didYouKnow: On clear days the overlook offers views west across Avra Valley toward the Ironwood Forest area.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky bajadas and washes, especially after spring rain
animals.viewingTip: If you spot one, admire it from several feet away and never handle it — its bite is rare but medically serious, and it's illegal in Arizona to touch or collect one.
animals.didYouKnow: Gila monsters spend an estimated 95% of their lives underground and can survive on just a few large meals a year.

animals.whereToLook: Desert scrub and washes near trailheads
animals.viewingTip: Give a javelina herd plenty of room, especially if young are present — they travel in tight family groups and can act defensively if they feel cornered; never feed them.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite their pig-like look, javelinas are peccaries, a separate family more closely related to hippos than to pigs.

animals.whereToLook: Open trail edges and low desert scrub
animals.viewingTip: Roadrunners are usually unbothered by quiet observers at a normal trail distance — pause and watch rather than chasing after one for a closer look.
animals.didYouKnow: Roadrunners can reach speeds of up to 20 mph on foot and rarely fly except to escape danger.

animals.whereToLook: Saguaro cavities throughout the Cactus Forest
animals.viewingTip: Watch nest cavities from a distance with binoculars rather than approaching the saguaro — repeated close visits can cause the pair to abandon the nest.
animals.didYouKnow: The cavities Gila woodpeckers carve into saguaros are later reused by elf owls, purple martins, and other cavity-nesting species.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky slopes in the Tucson Mountain District
animals.viewingTip: Never pick up a desert tortoise — when frightened it may void its bladder, losing water it needs to survive for months; simply step back and let it move on undisturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: A desert tortoise can store enough water in its bladder to last through most of the dry season.

animals.whereToLook: Open desert flats and wash corridors
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy coyote sightings from the trail with binoculars and never feed or try to call one in — habituated coyotes become a safety problem for both people and the animal.
animals.didYouKnow: Coyotes in the Sonoran Desert often den in old badger burrows or dense wash vegetation.

animals.whereToLook: Saguaro stands and open desert near the Cactus Forest
animals.viewingTip: Watch hunting groups with binoculars from a distance — Harris's hawks are one of the few raptors that hunt cooperatively in family groups, and a scope will reveal more of the behavior than getting close ever could.
animals.didYouKnow: Harris's hawks sometimes stack on top of one another on a single saguaro, a behavior nicknamed 'backstacking' that helps them scan for prey.

animals.whereToLook: Cholla and saguaro stands throughout the park
animals.viewingTip: Look and listen for its harsh, rattling call from the trail rather than reaching into cholla or saguaro nests to look inside — both the spines and a disturbed nest can hurt bird and hiker alike.
animals.didYouKnow: Arizona's state bird builds football-shaped nests tucked deep inside cholla cacti, using the spines as a natural predator deterrent.
